title: Challenges for higher education in the era of widespread access to Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines how widespread access to generative AI systems, especially tools such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, is challenging traditional higher education. The authors aim to discuss both the opportunities and risks of generative AI in university teaching and learning, including its usefulness for information acquisition, writing, problem solving, and programming, as well as concerns about hallucinations, misinformation, academic dishonesty, and erosion of critical thinking. The paper also considers broader implications for curriculum redesign, digital literacy, and the future role of universities and educators.

The empirical component is a survey of 143 university students drawn from multiple universities and disciplines. The survey asks about students’ prior use of AI tools, purposes for using ChatGPT and other systems, trust in AI-generated content, willingness to interact with chatbots, opinions about AI in education, and attitudes toward AI partially replacing teachers or grading exams. The paper also includes a conceptual discussion of generative AI capabilities across text, image, and sound generation, and uses an example of an AI-generated factual error to illustrate the problem of hallucinations.

The population studied consists of higher education students, including both bachelor’s and master’s students, in fields such as computer science, management, administration, and related areas. The context is higher education rather than K-12, and the study is framed around university transformation in response to pervasive generative AI. The participant pool appears to be based in Poland, given the institutional affiliations and publication context, though the survey is described as including students from diverse universities.

The main conclusions are that students are already using generative AI extensively, generally support allowing and teaching AI use in universities, but often overestimate their ability to detect AI errors. The authors argue that universities should not simply prohibit AI, but should adapt by strengthening factual knowledge, critical thinking, digital literacy, and responsible AI use. They emphasize that examinations should verify students’ own knowledge without AI assistance, and that higher education must prepare students to work with AI while avoiding overreliance on statistically generated outputs that may contain convincing falsehoods.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed survey study with descriptive analysis, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental evaluation and provides no controlled comparison of learning outcomes. It offers some empirical evidence but only one of the three main credibility criteria for strong causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows unclear practical impact: students perceive benefits and institutional relevance, but the evidence is descriptive and mixed, with no reported effect sizes or demonstrated improvements in academic outcomes. It is therefore best classified as unclear impact rather than proven positive or negative impact.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based examination of university students' use and perceptions of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT/GPT-4 for educational tasks including information search, problem solving, essay generation, summarization, translation, and class preparation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports survey results from 143 university students on perceptions of generative AI in higher education. A majority supported allowing and teaching AI use in universities (55%), and 76% believed AI systems would be useful in education in the future, but students were divided on whether AI tools might replace teachers and 51% opposed AI grading of exams. No causal estimates or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student survey responses on perceptions of AI integration, teacher replacement, and AI grading in higher education

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using ChatGPT for efficiency-oriented academic tasks such as finding solutions to problems (63%), information search (62%), programming (52%), and preparing for classes, homework, projects, and exams. These findings indicate perceived productivity benefits, but the study did not experimentally compare performance or time savings against a non-AI condition and reported no effect sizes.
finding.measure: Self-reported uses of ChatGPT for academic task completion and preparation

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents indirect evidence suggesting risks to critical thinking and verification skills: although 50% of students said they verify dubious AI-generated content and 24% said they always scrutinize it, only 21% detected a major factual error in a GPT-generated biography, while 50.7% failed to identify it. Among students claiming alertness or consistent verification, nearly half still missed the error (47.8% and 45.7%, respectively), suggesting overconfidence and weak real-world evaluation of AI outputs. No causal identification or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy in detecting factual hallucination in AI-generated text; self-reported trust and verification behavior
